articles.title: How Was the Cold War Won?
articles.content:
Peace Through Strength: How Reagan's Military Buildup Won the Cold War, by Roger Zakheim, Regnery, 472 pages, $40
With Peace Through Strength, Roger Zakheim, the director of the Ronald Reagan Institute, makes a valiant effort to put an old foreign policy idea in attractive new packaging. His principal thesis is that President Ronald Reagan's adoption of a tougher, more assertive foreign policy, especially a concerted military buildup, overawed the Soviet Union and ultimately produced a less confrontational leadership in the Kremlin under Mikhail Gorbachev. Indeed, he argues, the Reagan administration's displays of military power were a major causal factor in the subsequent dissolution of the USSR itself. America's victory strategy in the Cold War, Zakheim contends, should be a model for U.S. leadership today.
Peace Through Strength does contain some useful insights about the Reagan administration's stewardship of foreign policy. It also offers an extremely informative account of the ideological and bureaucratic struggle between two major Republican factions. One of those factions—led by David Stockman, the youthful director of the Office of Management and Budget—was passionately committed to balancing the budget and reducing the federal government's size, power, and expense; it sought to restrain military spending as well as domestic outlays. The competing faction, led by Secretary of Defense Caspar Weinberger, gave top priority to building a larger and more powerful military. To achieve that, they were willing to sacrifice most of the other goals on the conservative movement's wish list.
Weinberger's exceptionally close personal relationship with Reagan, along with the defense secretary's substantially greater experience at bureaucratic infighting, ultimately helped produce victory for the hawkish faction. Reagan's own inclinations were an even more important factor.
Zakheim notes that "Stockman was right" to be uneasy about the evolution of the internal struggle regarding the budget. "For Reagan, funding the military buildup was a matter of principle. It was a priority with no equal. According to Stockman, this was the turning point where he 'ceased to believe that the Reagan Revolution was possible.' What he seemed to fail to understand was that the essence of the Reagan Revolution was that Reagan prioritized the military buildup above all else."
Nearly 50 years later, the triumph of Weinberger and his fellow hawks still largely defines the GOP's policy priorities. A commitment to high levels of military spending trumps virtually any competing objective in the Republican Party.
Peace Through Strength makes the best case for its general thesis in the passages discussing the Reagan administration's handling of policy during the final years of the Cold War in Europe, the longstanding confrontation's principal theater. Yet even when he focuses narrowly on U.S.-Soviet relations, the author tends to overgeneralize and overreach. Zakheim attributes the fading of the Cold War in the late 1980s almost entirely to the impact of Reagan's military buildup. But while that undoubtedly played a role in the changes in the Kremlin's policies, it is a mistake to minimize, much less ignore, the role of other factors. After Gorbachev came to power in Moscow, he headed a relatively youthful policy team that was inclined to adopt economic reforms, to allow a more open society, and to move toward a more flexible, less confrontational foreign policy. The pervasive inefficiencies in the ossified Soviet system were nearly impossible to ignore any longer.
Without those ideological changes, it is improbable that Moscow would have pursued a new, more cooperative and constructive relationship with the West—even given the intimidating aura of Washington's indisputable military superiority. Indeed, the Reagan-era military buildup might have triggered an outright confrontation akin to the Berlin standoff or the Cuban missile crisis if the White House had faced an old-style Soviet regime that felt increasingly beleaguered.
Zakheim finds himself on even shakier analytical ground when he tries to apply the supposed lessons of the Reagan military buildup to the geopolitical challenges of today's world. Bipolarity was still the dominant characteristic of the international system in the 1980s, and the Soviet Union remained America's only credible strategic challenger. Moreover, the USSR was a one-dimensional challenger. It possessed substantial military capabilities, but its economy was a chronic dumpster fire, and the gains that the Kremlin's deceptive diplomacy achieved in the Third World from the 1950s through the 1970s had begun to erode. One wag—there is no universally accepted source, but the line is often attributed to West German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt—captured the reality of the Soviet Union as a one-dimensional "superpower" when he called the country little more than "Upper Volta with nuclear weapons."
The world of the 2020s is vastly more complex. Military and diplomatic multipolarity have now emerged to join economic multipolarity as a global reality. Secondary but important geopolitical players such as Brazil and India must be taken into account by U.S. leaders and treated with respect on a wide range of strategic issues. Russia is a weak shadow of its Soviet predecessor, but the People's Republic of China has emerged as a strategic peer competitor to the United States. Moreover, Beijing's capabilities are far more sophisticated and multidimensional than Moscow could have ever hoped to muster during the Cold War. Trying to overawe or intimidate China the way that Zakheim believes Reagan's buildup did to the USSR would be a blueprint for national bankruptcy.
Even worse, such a myopic strategy could well trigger the kind of catastrophic great-power war with China that U.S. leaders were able to avoid during the long confrontation with the Soviets. Even daunting military strength does not necessarily lead to peace. Such vast power can produce a range of outcomes, some of which have the potential to be dreadful for nearly all concerned.
Zakheim seems oblivious to that danger. He reflexively repeats the cliché that democracies "are non-expansionist in nature, with political leadership held accountable to an electorate that prioritizes their economic needs." Democracies may be "non-expansionist" if that concept is confined to recent acquisitions of formal colonies, but Britain, France, and the United States all possessed democratic systems when they acquired their earlier empires. The notion that democracies are inherently non-expansionist is clearly false. More importantly, democracies can and have engaged in toxic aggressive military behavior in other ways. Washington's numerous and gratuitous recent wars of choice fatally undermine the "peaceful democracies" thesis. Moreover, that unpleasant reality is now widely recognized by populations around the world.
So Zakheim's implicit assumption that current or future U.S. military buildups will promote peace rather than war is defective at its core. Other countries may well see themselves as potential targets of Washington's coercion and interpret such a buildup as extremely threatening. There could be a powerful temptation for such a country to respond with its own buildup or, worse, to take preemptive military actions.
Given what the world has witnessed since the end of the Cold War, displays of even greater U.S. military strength are more likely to bring war, not Zakheim's peaceful utopia. Reagan's military buildup was not the main reason the democratic capitalist West won the Cold War. Today's buildup is worse, since it is both needlessly dangerous and counterproductive. It is not likely to usher in even a brief era of peace.
The post How Was the Cold War Won? appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Supreme Court To Weigh Trump's Unilateral Suspension of Asylum Protections at Southern Border
articles.content:
The U.S. Supreme Court's current term has been a bit lacking so far when it comes to high-profile cases. I don't mean to imply any lack of important cases—indeed, just last week the Court heard oral arguments in a major case about holding federal officials to account for constitutional rights violations—rather, what I mean is that we haven't really yet seen the kind of headline-grabbing legal disputes that capture national attention and send political activists into overdrive.
But that may be about to change. On Friday, the justices agreed to hear arguments in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a case arising from the Trump administration's unilateral executive suspension of asylum protections for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. Much like last term's big showdown over tariffs, the key question in this case is whether President Donald Trump is guilty of wielding authority that properly belongs to a different branch of the federal government. At the very least, a SCOTUS fight over immigration and presidential overreach in the waning age of Trump has the makings of a blockbuster case.
Under federal immigration law, persons who are unlawfully present in the United States are subject to removal proceedings. At the same time, federal law also says that such persons may attempt to obtain relief from removal by seeking asylum, or by seeking withholding from removal, under either the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) or the Convention Against Torture, on the grounds that they would face persecution or torture if deported.
The Trump administration, however, asserts that it may unilaterally suspend the asylum and withholding from removal protections for persons who unlawfully crossed the U.S.-Mexico border. According to a January 2025 presidential proclamation, "the President's inherent powers to control the borders of the United States, including those deriving from his authority to control the foreign affairs of the United States, necessarily include the ability to prevent the physical entry of aliens involved in an invasion into the United States, and to rapidly repatriate them to an alternative location."
In April 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected this executive argument. "Our task is to determine whether Congress has granted the Executive the authority to remove foreign individuals present in the United States without adhering to the removal procedures or providing the substantive removal protections that Congress prescribed in the INA," the appellate court said. "We conclude that the INA's text, structure, and history make clear that in supplying power to suspend entry by Presidential proclamation, Congress did not intend to grant the Executive the expansive removal authority it asserts."
It is that loss before the D.C. Circuit that the Trump administration has now persuaded the Supreme Court to review.
In addition to reviewing the statutory question decided by the D.C. Circuit, it is possible the Supreme Court may also wade into the underlying argument over what counts as an "invasion" for constitutional purposes, as Trump's assertion of "inherent" executive power in this case rests on Trump's view that the president is doubly empowered to act in this manner because an "invasion" is occurring at the southern border. That view from Trump is a version of the oft-heard argument that normal constitutional limits on the president should be weakened or even removed when the president is acting in the name of foreign affairs or national security.
My guess is that the Supreme Court will avoid this constitutional minefield and stick to the safer grounds of statutory interpretation. But an outbreak of broader constitutional conflict is possible.
The post Supreme Court To Weigh Trump's Unilateral Suspension of Asylum Protections at Southern Border appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Before the Falklands War, Islanders and Argentines Were Neighbors
articles.content:
Beyond the War: Argentines and Islanders in an Unknown Falklands, by Sebastián Carassai, Cambridge University Press, 372 pages, $50
Pamela McLeod and her husband, Reynaldo Reid, set off for Buenos Aires for a belated honeymoon in November 1970, likely hoping for a little privacy, relaxation, and time together. They got anything but.
Their marriage, it turned out, was politically irresistible. McLeod was a Falkland Islander, and Reid was Argentine. This was gold to an Argentine press eager to present the couple as evidence of the bonds between the British-held islands and Argentina. When the couple arrived in Buenos Aires, reporters and cameramen were waiting. The honeymoon became a 15-day publicity tour through television studios, ministries, and political offices.
The growth of Argentine nationalism, and Britain's increasing separation of the islands from the mainland, eventually allowed "the relationship between countries to displace the relationship between neighbors," writes Sebastián Carassai in Beyond the War. Carassai's book reminds us of the relationships between Argentines and Falklanders that existed beyond—and were eventually eclipsed by—their governments' competing nationalisms. (Those who side with Argentina would call the islands the Malvinas.)
Reid was emblematic of the region's blurred borders before the 1982 Falklands War. His father was Scottish and his mother English; he was born in Argentina, had Chilean sisters and an Argentine brother, and later spent much of his life with McLeod in the Falklands capital of Stanley.
The couple had seven daughters and two sons together, the youngest of whom was born in 1981. In Stanley, Reid became an informal Argentine delegate, and he co-ran what is now the third-oldest bar in the islands. After living in Stanley for more than a decade, he told the Argentine press that the island community had accepted him as just another member.
McLeod, who grew up in the Falklands' rural countryside, was an orphan brought up by families that took turns raising her. After living a "homeless life," as she described it to Carassai, she moved on to married life in Stanley. In April 1982, a few days after the Argentine invasion of the Falkland Islands, McLeod and seven of her children flew to Argentina to avoid the conflict.
Her eldest two children were already studying on the continent. The family intended to return to the islands once the crisis was over—the eldest daughter, who was studying to become a teacher in Buenos Aires, told a TV program that she planned to work at a school in Stanley. Yet the family ended up staying: "We went to spend a few days and stayed for thirty years," McLeod told Carassai.
After her husband's death, McLeod enjoyed the network of support she received from Jehovah's Witnesses while looking after her family of "refugees." Starting in the '90s, many of her children, now married to Argentines, began moving back to the Falklands. McLeod, with a new Argentine husband, also moved back to Stanley.
They weren't the only border-crossing individuals whose lives were disrupted by the clashing nationalisms. James Peck, an artist from the Falklands, was married to an Argentine woman and had two children, but he became estranged from his wife and kids in the late 2000s. Amid the family crisis, he was offered and accepted an Argentine identity card. The ceremony became an extraordinary political spectacle. It was chaired by then-president of Argentina, Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, and the official propaganda for the event described Peck as the first islander "to receive the Argentine DNI (Documento Nacional de Identidad) after the conflict." According to Carassai, the entire situation was "overwhelming" for Peck, who was considered a traitor by many Falkland Islanders. The Argentine government took advantage of a father in distress and used him to score political points.
"I feel like Argentina has cast a big shadow over my soul," Peck told The Guardian in 2016. "I had one thing on my mind: to fix my family and move on." After four years, Peck cut up the Argentine document, posted a photo of the pieces on Facebook, and returned to Stanley. "I realized, after, that real people did not seem to matter; it was all about making a statement, about the islands, and they had this prize," he told The Guardian.
Carassai spoke with islanders from across society (including politicians, business owners, and retirees), in addition to doing archival work. The interviews in his epilogue tell human stories too often lost in historical accounts of the Falklands, which tend to focus exclusively on the war; his conversations reveal a relationship far more complicated than the stories told by both the Argentine and the British governments.
Outside of the messy human accounts revealed through marriages, friendships, and migration, Beyond the War explores the economic ties that inevitably developed between the islands and the South American mainland. Falkland Islanders, who often referred to the nearby mainland simply as "the coast," were instrumental in establishing sheep farming, working on Patagonian estancias (ranches), and transferring agricultural expertise across the South Atlantic.
Indeed, the Falkland Islands and Patagonia were economically intertwined long before the sovereignty dispute came to dominate relations. In the late 19th century, Argentina actively recruited Falklanders to help with economic development in Patagonia. In 1886, the governor of Santa Cruz, Carlos María Moyano, married a Falkland Islander, Ethel Turner. With support from Buenos Aires, Moyano promised cheap leases for any farmer who would move to the scarcely populated Santa Cruz. Surnames familiar in the islands—Halliday, Rudd, Scott, Blake, Patterson, Hamilton, Waldron, Wood—also became common in Patagonia. Many of these migrants brought sheep-farming expertise to Argentina, helping to establish prosperous estancias. The largest ranch, Cóndor, covered 200,000 hectares and became the headquarters of the Patagonian Sheep Farming Company, which for many years was the most important livestock company in southern Argentina.
Trade between the communities went both ways. The Falkland Islands Gazette reported on the importation of animals (particularly horses) from "Patagonia," "Argentina," and "South America." By the 1970s, Argentina was supplying the islands with coal, oil, kerosene, and diesel for domestic use. Carassai describes the Argentine construction of an airstrip as "the most important work," which cost about 750,000 pounds (more than $12 million in today's money) and made regular air links with Argentina possible. In 1971, the British and Argentine governments signed the Communications Agreement, and regular flights became commonplace. Carassai argues that these projects were intended not only to improve life on the islands but also to signal to the islanders, Britain, and the United Nations that Argentina could be trusted "to look after the interests of the island population."
The introduction of regular flights had an enormous impact on the Falklanders. Children could go to Argentina for secondary school, patients traveled to Argentine hospitals, Argentine teachers worked in Stanley, and tourists began arriving from the mainland. Less than a year after regular flights began, The Falkland Islands Times cautioned readers about the pace of change.
"Although there were disadvantages of being so out off," Rev. Robin Forrester wrote of the era before the Communications Agreement, "there were also advantages, not the least of which was the fact that strangers couldn't creep in unawares. Nowadays, with a plane service each week, strangers abound and the pace of life is speeding up."
Beyond the War provides a rather different historical account of the Falkland Islands than is most commonly understood. Unfortunately, the islands are rarely thought of outside the 1982 war and are almost always discussed through the prism of the sovereignty dispute. Indeed, just this year President Javier Milei renewed Argentina's claim to the islands, pledging tougher sanctions on companies operating around the Falklands and more funding for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego. Prior to the war, the territory barely registered in the British public imagination at all; few Britons could have located it on a map, and some servicemen dispatched to the conflict initially assumed that the Falklands were somewhere off the coast of Scotland.
This book is valuable precisely because it recovers what the nationalistic framings obscure. Europeans established their first permanent settlement on the Falklands in 1764. There is a long, rich, and complicated history of migration, trade, tourism, and family ties across the region. Argentines lived in Stanley, Falkland Islanders worked in Patagonia, children crossed the sea for school, patients for medical treatment, and tourists for holidays. This history did not make the sovereignty dispute disappear. But neither did the sovereignty dispute make war itself inevitable.
Carassai's achievement is to recover a time when the British and Argentine governments may have had a disagreement about territory, but Falkland Islanders and Argentines could still be neighbors. Borders are drawn by governments, but life across them is rarely so neat.

"I realized, after, that real people did not seem to matter; it was all about making a statement, about the islands, and they had this prize," he told The Guardian.

Carassai spoke with islanders from across society (including politicians, business owners, and retirees), in addition to doing archival work. The interviews in his epilogue tell human stories too often lost in historical accounts of the Falklands, which tend to focus exclusively on the war; his conversations reveal a relationship far more complicated than the stories told by both the Argentine and the British governments.

Outside of the messy human accounts revealed through marriages, friendships, and migration, Beyond the War explores the economic ties that inevitably developed between the islands and the South American mainland. Falkland Islanders, who often referred to the nearby mainland simply as "the coast," were instrumental in establishing sheep farming, working on Patagonian estancias (ranches), and transferring agricultural expertise across the South Atlantic.

Indeed, the Falkland Islands and Patagonia were economically intertwined long before the sovereignty dispute came to dominate relations. In the late 19th century, Argentina actively recruited Falklanders to help with economic development in Patagonia. In 1886, the governor of Santa Cruz, Carlos María Moyano, married a Falkland Islander, Ethel Turner. With support from Buenos Aires, Moyano promised cheap leases for any farmer who would move to the scarcely populated Santa Cruz. Surnames familiar in the islands—Halliday, Rudd, Scott, Blake, Patterson, Hamilton, Waldron, Wood—also became common in Patagonia. Many of these migrants brought sheep-farming expertise to Argentina, helping to establish prosperous estancias. The largest ranch, Cóndor, covered 200,000 hectares and became the headquarters of the Patagonian Sheep Farming Company, which for many years was the most important livestock company in southern Argentina.

Trade between the communities went both ways. The Falkland Islands Gazette reported on the importation of animals (particularly horses) from "Patagonia," "Argentina," and "South America." By the 1970s, Argentina was supplying the islands with coal, oil, kerosene, and diesel for domestic use. Carassai describes the Argentine construction of an airstrip as "the most important work," which cost about 750,000 pounds (more than $12 million in today's money) and made regular air links with Argentina possible. In 1971, the British and Argentine governments signed the Communications Agreement, and regular flights became commonplace. Carassai argues that these projects were intended not only to improve life on the islands but also to signal to the islanders, Britain, and the United Nations that Argentina could be trusted "to look after the interests of the island population."

The introduction of regular flights had an enormous impact on the Falklanders. Children could go to Argentina for secondary school, patients traveled to Argentine hospitals, Argentine teachers worked in Stanley, and tourists began arriving from the mainland. Less than a year after regular flights began, The Falkland Islands Times cautioned readers about the pace of change.

"Although there were disadvantages of being so out off," Rev. Robin Forrester wrote of the era before the Communications Agreement, "there were also advantages, not the least of which was the fact that strangers couldn't creep in unawares. Nowadays, with a plane service each week, strangers abound and the pace of life is speeding up."

Beyond the War provides a rather different historical account of the Falkland Islands than is most commonly understood. Unfortunately, the islands are rarely thought of outside the 1982 war and are almost always discussed through the prism of the sovereignty dispute. Indeed, just this year President Javier Milei renewed Argentina's claim to the islands, pledging tougher sanctions on companies operating around the Falklands and more funding for a naval base in Tierra del Fuego. Prior to the war, the territory barely registered in the British public imagination at all; few Britons could have located it on a map, and some servicemen dispatched to the conflict initially assumed that the Falklands were somewhere off the coast of Scotland.

This book is valuable precisely because it recovers what the nationalistic framings obscure. Europeans established their first permanent settlement on the Falklands in 1764. There is a long, rich, and complicated history of migration, trade, tourism, and family ties across the region. Argentines lived in Stanley, Falkland Islanders worked in Patagonia, children crossed the sea for school, patients for medical treatment, and tourists for holidays. This history did not make the sovereignty dispute disappear. But neither did the sovereignty dispute make war itself inevitable.

Carassai's achievement is to recover a time when the British and Argentine governments may have had a disagreement about territory, but Falkland Islanders and Argentines could still be neighbors. Borders are drawn by governments, but life across them is rarely so neat.

articles.content:
Osceola County, Florida, sheriff's deputy Joseph Billittier was arrested after investigators determined that he lied about being attacked by a 67-year-old woman during a DUI arrest. A motorist called 911 to report a woman driving the wrong way on a road in Kissimmee before she ended up in the median. Deputies arrested her for DUI, but by the time she reached the jail, she had sustained injuries and needed to be assessed by a doctor. Billittier claimed she battered him while he was placing her in his patrol car, but after reviewing his body camera and dashcam footage, investigators determined not only that she had not attacked him but that he had used unnecessary force. The woman had previously broken her collarbone and was wearing a sling on one arm. Billittier faces charges including battery against a person 65 or older.
